I refer, of course, to the Salvation Army. Members will, I know, want to acknowledge the presence in the Speaker's Gallery this morning of the Canadian Commander, Commissioner Edgar Grinsted, Mrs. Commissioner Grinsted and other senior officers of this great and vital organization which is this year celebrating a century of service to God and to man.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON ONE HUNDRED YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON ONE HUNDRED YEARS OF SERVICE
speechtext:
It was just 100 years ago that its founder, William Booth, first stood on Mile End Waste in the east end of London, England, in the midst of the degradation and disorganization of the industrial revolution and proclaimed the age old message that gave birth to the Salvation Army.
In the intervening century the Army has extended its good work into all parts of the world. I am sure all hon. Members, particularly those who are war veterans, will be entirely familiar with the fine work of this organization in evangelical and social welfare endeavour, and will join with me in wishing them Godspeed as they continue their great work of mercy into a second century of service to their fellow men.
May I add that the hon. member for Bran-don-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), who is himself a leading member of the Salvation Army in Canada, has asked me to call attention to the special Service of Commemoration that is being held this evening in Christ Church Cathedral at 8 p.m. This service will take place in the immediate presence of their Excellencies the Governor General and Madame Vanier, and Commissioner Grinsted will be the guest speaker. The hon. Member for Brandon-Souris has reminded me that hon. Members of this House are cordially invited to attend and share in the fellowship of this important anniversary occasion.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON ONE HUNDRED YEARS OF SERVICE

The Address-Mr. Favreau their speeches, John Cabot and Jacques Cartier had stepped out of the history books and sat in this house to listen to their respective posthumous proteges, if I may call them thus, they would surely have had a long discussion to determine which of those two young and brilliant members had been more eloquent and convincing. Being both great partisans of truth, I am sure they would have agreed as we all do here that both speeches were, each in its own way, as politically sincere and eloquent one as the other.

Mr. Speaker, I am proud-and I thank God and my fellow citizens for giving me the opportunity, despite some difficulties and sometimes also, perhaps, the cruelty of politics, especially for a beginner, to work on this team with the group of Liberals which faithfully surround me, for the greatest prosperity and happiness of the Canadian people. And all this under the dynamic leadership of a man who will undoubtedly be remembered in history as one of the great prime ministers of our country and certainly also as one of our most genuine Canadian patriots, the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Pearson).
Mr. Speaker, at the very beginning of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) engaged in a biting speech, the skilful looseness of which was only surpassed by the outrageous series of contradictions to be found in it.
In that speech, which was certainly not a model of logical arrangement, the Leader of the Opposition, saw fit to bravely blame the Government-these are not the very words he used, but their inner meaning-for gathering in the speech from the throne a series of pieces of legislation almost without any link, intended merely to blind us to the facts and to serve electoral purposes.
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne as presented to the people of this country has not been written casually. It is a thoroughly thought out document, which contains a legislative program quite in accordance with the traditional thinking of the Liberal party in this country.
When one takes the trouble to analyse that speech from the throne, to study it objectively, one sees it, first of all, as the neces-

April 9. 1965

The Address-Mr. Favreau sary extension and the natural result of the mandate given to the Liberal party by the Canadian people at the general election of April 1963; second, it is the normal extension and natural result of the carrying out of the measures which this government succeeded in having passed by both houses and in putting into effect in a brief period of two years, despite the filibustering of an opposition which persisted in obstructing the work of parliament.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, even if the official opposition in particular is green-eyed with jealousy over the speech from the Throne it meets the interests and wishes of every Canadian to such an extent that if any citizen of this country, with a knowledge of Canadian politics and of the achievements of the present Government in the last two years, had endeavoured to draft it beforehand, he would necessarily have included therein all the social and other measures which it contains.
Indeed, the speech from the Throne embodies remarkably well at least three of the great ideals which, traditionally, Liberal governments have pursued and which they endeavour to apply in the best interests of the citizens of this country: in the first place, a genuine Canadian patriotism, second, an unflagging concern for our economic stability and development, a finally, the wish to see the triumph of social justice, in its broadest sense, in this country and for every individual.
If they examine every measure proposed in the speech from the Throne, the hon. members will realize that they all fit within the framework of one of those three great ideals.
In view of the short time at my disposal, I will discuss more particularly the three proposed measures which specially fall within the purview of the department I have the honour to direct. In my opinion, those three measures are desirable so that Canada can maintain and enrich its civilization.
They all come under the banner of justice in a liberal society, with a small "1".
Justice is the respect of the rights of everyone and, in a modern world such as ours, justice would and should reconcile the con-


current interests of every Canadian, as well as the interests of the individual with those of the state.
Such a synthesis was difficult to work out, to effect, but it will be found that the three measures in question will carry it into effect if they are passed. Their purpose is to ensure first of all, in all fairness, the freedom the individual and in this connection, I shall deal briefly with the "ombudsman". I shall then refer to the protection of society and say a few words also about our research in the correctional field. Finally, I shall deal with the Canadianization of our country and make a few brief remarks about the proposed amendment formula to the Canadian constitution.
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne raises the question as to whether it is advisable to institute in our country an ombudsman and if so, what will be the terms of reference of the royal commission to study and report on matters respecting the administrative courts.
The growth of government business and services has made it necessary, in the interests of the citizens in our modern world of 1965, to a tremendous administrative machinery and a large increase in the number of civil servants. This was necessary because nowadays, the state is of necessity required to provide a great number of services that individuals had to provide for themselves in the past. The state is now taking a great number of decisions which hitherto belonged exclusively to the private citizen himself.
It is a fact, as found in several countries of the world, that this administrative machinery actually stands between the individual and the state. The private citizen has often been scared and sometimes completely overwhelmed. We have reached a point where, in some cases and in certain ways, people feel their personality is being perhaps crushed by the growth of legislative services. They feel a bit awed by this machinery which, of necessity, bears a somewhat impersonal character. That is why I think we must make sure that the citizens of this country where, after all, every government service is meant for them and to serve their own interests, are not hit on the rebound, so to speak, by a reaction which could leave the impression that their security and personal interests are affected to any extent. I think the citizen's confidence in the administration and the civil service must be restored or at least maintained. At the same time, and quite properly, civil servants should also feel nearer the
April 9, 1965

people and have not only the impression but the assurance that they enjoy the respect and confidence of the citizenry.
Some countries have already tried, and the experience varied from one country to the other, to overcome such difficulties and dangers by appointing a most impartial and independent officer who looks first of all for simplicity in all procedures. This officer is responsible and reports to parliament; in some countries he is called a parliamentary commissioner and, in others, an ombudsman.
I do not intend to recall the history of the ombudsman, I will briefly outline his duties. In short, an ombudsman could be a parliamentary officer whose function is to receive and examine complaints from Canadian citizens who may feel that they have been wronged by the authorities or that their rights are being encroached upon by some civil servants or departmental officials through misuse of authority. The function of that parliamentary commissioner or ombudsman would be, therefore, to examine the complaint and, if he deems it unwarranted to convince the plaintiff that he has not in fact been ill treated or placed in an untenable position and that the state was not unfair toward him; on the other hand, if the complaint is warranted, he would make to the state or to its officials the necessary recommendations so that the situation may be remedied.

The Address-Mr. Crouse
I have read the Speech from the Throne in the hope I would find therein some special recognition of the social and economic ills that continue to plague the Atlantic Provinces. However, in this instance, the Liberals have run true to form and again ignored the Maritime area. The Throne Speech contains a mountain of proposed legislation, of which only a small part could vaguely be construed as applying to our area. Why was there no recognition given to the needs of our Maritime universities? Their financial plight should be of some concern to this Government. The university grants are still administered by the Federal authorities on the basis of the population of a province, divided into the size of the subsidy which the Federal Government makes available. The province then divides this sum by the number of university students within its borders, thereby determining the per student grant.
This method has resulted in a greater share going to the larger and growing provinces, while the Atlantic Provinces, especially Nova Scotia with its high student enrolment in its numerous universities, has received a smaller proportion of the grant than any province in Canada. The cost of maintaining and expanding Nova Scotia's universities is constantly increasing, mainly as a result of the actions of this Government and its 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. With costs spiraling, it may be necessary for economic reasons to restrict the enrolment of students from other regions of Canada. It would indeed be regrettable if this action became necessary. I think the Government should take another look at this matter immediately. A more equitable formula would be to make the total Federal subsidy available on a national basis with the grants to be provided to the various provinces based on the number of students attending universities in that province.
In the economic area surely this Government, which has 100 per cent support from the Province of Newfoundland-even if the Cabinet Minister's origin as a Newfoundlander is questionable-must give an answer to the Atlantic problems.

One of these, the "designated areas" program, she disclosed for the first time, had resulted in some 20 firms indicating to the Government interest in establishing new plants or new production facilities in the Atlantic provinces....

Then she got a little bit political and tried to attribute much of the improvement to the policies of the Federal Government.
If the Minister were less interested in gathering bouquets for herself and the Government, she would realize that much of the credit for the present industrial revolution taking place in Nova Scotia must go to Hon. Robert Stanfield and his hard working cabinet. This dedicated group of men are leaving no stone unturned in their efforts to bring new employment opportunities to Nova Scotians. As I have said, in pursuing their goals in Nova Scotia the Provincial Cabinet, led by Premier Stanfield, must not only endeavour to bring in new industries but they must help provide an economic climate that will help hold and expand existing primary industries.
In order to obtain these goals the Premier of Nova Scotia, along with other Atlantic Province Premiers, requires additional assistance from the federal treasury. I say this because unemployment in the Atlantic Provinces is not what the minister told that group in Montreal, but in fact is higher than in any other part of Canada. The Daily Gleaner in its editorial on March 18, pointed out the seriousness of the problem, and I quote:
The mid-February employment report contained bad news for the Atlantic region. Unemployment stood at 13 per cent, a jump of 2.2 per cent from the figure of a month earlier. ...
The Atlantic region's jobless totalled 78,000, as compared with 64,000 in mid-January... . This shows conclusively that whatever is maintaining relative prosperity in every other part of Canada is not functioning in the Maritimes.
In mid-winter the primary industries, vital to the Atlantic economy, are operating at low ebb, and the region has only made the first gestures at developing the network of secondary industries to take up the employment slack.
So we have this veritable army of the unemployed, who, with their families must be sustained by various forms of relief and social assistance.
The shame and the folly of this situation should spur everyone concerned to a sustained effort to end this situation of regional inequality once and for all.
I repeat that the unemployment figure is 13 per cent, not 7.8 per cent. Perhaps it is time we reconstituted the truth squad.
When you examine these figures and compare them with the total claims for unemployment insurance at the end of January, which numbered 547,800, it is easy to note the higher percentage of unemployment and unemployed in the Maritime Provinces in relation to the rest of Canada.
Under such circumstances it is not difficult to understand the anger and despair of Maritimers, who take exception to the tariff wall with which we have surrounded such industries as the assembly plants of United States automobile manufacturers in Ontario. We have been told repeatedly that the wall is there to safeguard the jobs of workers. As a result, Canadians pay approximately one third more for their cars than Americans
April 9, 1965

The Address-Mr. Crouse do, and people in the Maritimes, as a result of greater distance from the assembly plants and the higher freight rates, must pay more for their cars than citizens of Quebec or Ontario. We are told in the Throne Speech that in this session we will be asked to approve a resolution concerning the important agreement on the automobile industry recently concluded with the United States. Mr. Speaker, in all sincerity, I ask to whom is this agreement important? Since its terms have been announced, we have not seen or heard of any reduction in the price of automobiles to Canadian buyers, and since cars are no longer a luxury, but a necessity to the average Canadian, this should certainly be the objective of any change in the present legislation.
As I said earlier, we are told in the Maritimes we must pay more by way of tariffs on automobiles to protect the jobs of the workers. What about the workers in the Atlantic Provinces and their need for job protection? For some years, Maritimers enjoyed a preferred position on goods moving within the area and westbound from the Maritimes, but the disparity in present freight charges works a hardship on our primary and secondary industries, and when our products cannot be delivered competitively, our industries slacken or close down. It can truthfully be said that higher freight rates contribute to our unemployment condition.
Maritimers quite rightly ask, what can be done to improve the situation? Well, the Speech from the Throne promises comprehensive legislation to reform public regulation of the railways and to facilitate the adoption of the railway system to present and future needs. It seems to me that I have heard that song before.
For more than two years, transportation experts in the Department of Transport have worked out new railway legislation based on the MacPherson Commission's recommendations; but what happens? As soon as the public get an opportunity to look at these recommendations, and point out some of the faults in the proposals, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) does one of his well known flip-flops and says he was only flying a kite to gain public reaction. And all the while the Minister fiddles and fumbles, it is still possible for a stove manufacturer in Hamilton, Ontario, to ship his product to Montreal for approximately 75 cents per stove cheaper than a Nova Scotian producer in

Sackville can deliver a similar product over the same distance. Now this is not much per stove, but on volume business it soon runs into thousands of dollars. And this is only one side of the coin.
It must be remembered that Nova Scotian companies must pay considerably more freight charges on inbound raw materials. For example, the ship refitting yards in Lunenburg and Queens Counties, when fabricating equipment for ships or other industrial purposes, must pay over $1 more per 100 pounds of inbound freight charges on steel sheets as compared with a manufacturer in Hamilton. These extra freight costs price many of our Maritime manufacturers out of the market when competing for business in Central Canada, and I don't think we should allow anyone to fool us into thinking transportation costs are not the major key to our problems.
Now what is the answer? It of course lies in the fact that competitive freight rates have been set up as a result of producers being able to use water or highway transport in the Central Provinces as an alternative to the railroads. In my opinion, the economy and employment opportunities in the Atlantic Provinces, will always lag behind the rest of Canada, until the Federal Government recognizes the fact that improved transportation links are of prime importance, e (2:50 p.m.)
Lower cost freight charges on goods shipped westward is the key to survival of our primary and secondary industries in the Atlantic Provinces, and this can only be brought about by an improved highway system, with the Federal Government working in co-operation with the Provinces concerned. At present, the C.N.R. is the major hauler of freight, but it is endeavouring to cut down on its yearly deficit, and part of its program is to terminate service on what it considers uneconomical branch lines. These changes are proposed without too much consideration being given to the effect on the economy of these areas, but I ask the Government and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) which bill they think will be the highest, the one for subsidizing the railroads or the cost of dissolving industry and finding new homes and jobs for the people involved?
Mr. Speaker, we cannot go on ignoring the social and economic problems of the Atlantic Provinces. Canada, and the provinces concerned, cannot permit emigration to occur- which was one of the suggestions put forth as a solution to our problems by the present
April 9, 1965

Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) in his 1956 Royal Commission report on Canada's Economic Prospects. No good purpose can be served by endeavouring to build up one part of Canada on the one hand, while tearing it down with the other. There is only one answer, and it is for all the Governments concerned, acting in unison, to come to terms now on the simple question, "What does it take in dollars to help you expand your economy so that you can remain in the Atlantic Provinces?" It is futile to argue that this will cost the country money, for this is a certainty. But the cost of establishing new industry, and enabling Maritimers to stand on their own two feet, will indeed be small when compared with the alternative. In short, the present key industries of the Atlantic Provinces must be maintained in health and expanded, at least during a lengthy transition period while new economic areas are under development.
You might rightly ask, "Where do we begin?" The Speech from the Throne calls for improved measures for regional development, and states, "We will be asked to approve measures to aid industrial expansion in those areas requiring improved employment opportunities". I am in agreement with this particular proposal, and I would suggest that the Government give consideration to starting immediately on a multipurpose causeway dam from the Annapolis Valley shore at Cape Split to Fox River Point on the Cumberland shore across Minas Basin. This would serve to develop tidal power, and provide a transportation link as well as recreational facilities in the area. The Atlantic Development Board has been asked to undertake a feasibility study of this project, and if this study indicates the proposal is practical we already have the endorsation of Premier Stanfield on this project.
Just what is involved? The length of the dam between Cape Split and Fox River Point would be four miles, and in places it would be 200 feet deep. Engineers have estimated there would be 5 million kilowatts of power generated annually by such a project. The generators of this power could be similar to the ones used on the River Ranee in Britanny, France, which is the first commercial tidal power development in the world. These generators are essentially like small submarines set in tunnels at the bottom of the dam, and they would catch the surge and flow of tidal waters both entering and emptying Minas Basin.
The Address-Mr. Crouse
The recent trend in cheaper transmission costs would enable the power produced from this dam to be exported to the power-hungry markets of the United States, especially to New England, after the immediate needs of an expanded industrial complex in this area of Nova Scotia were satisfied. This proposed development for Minas Basin would be the largest single source of power in the world, and the future possibilities for industrial development would be virtually unlimited. We must also remember that the only money required for this project is the amount expended on the original construction. Once the dam is built and the generators installed, the electrical output will continue to be produced by the tides in perpetuity. We therefore need long term cheap money, loaned by the Federal Government, which in turn will be reflected in cheap power that will guarantee economic development in the entire area.
In addition to these benefits, the highway crossing the causeway would end the transportation bottleneck in the western part of Nova Scotia. For example it would no longer be necessary for trucks serving the industries in Liverpool, Bridgewater, Lunenburg, Ma-hone Bay or Chester to travel all the way to Halifax when en route to central Canadian markets with produce or manufactured products. These trucks could cut across the Province from Chester Basin through New Ross to Kentville, and crossing over the new causeway to Parrsboro they could cut off an estimated 100 miles on the highway route from the South Shore of Nova Scotia to Fredericton, New Brunswick.
At this point, I would like to propose another change. The Speech from the Throne states:
My Ministers attach great importance to Canada's neighbourly relationship with the United States and to the development of practical, mutually beneficial arrangements within that relationship.
In keeping with that lofty concept, I would suggest that the present administration start negotiations immediately with American authorities in order to gain early acceptance of our proposal for a corridor road through the State of Maine. This would be an exercise of our good neighbour policy, and would shorten the distance from the trans-Canada highway at Fredericton, New Brunswick, to Sherbrooke, Quebec, by 150 miles. This would bring Montreal to within a comfortable five-hour run from the Maritime border. Surely the cost to the Federal treasury of building this corridor road could not be termed excessive by anyone, when weighed against the
April 9, 1965

The Address-Mr. Crouse benefits this shorter highway route would bring to our primary and secondary industries in the Atlantic Provinces.
Mr. Speaker, this type of proposal should not be too difficult to negotiate with the Americans. We have co-operated with the Americans in the sale of B.C. power, we cooperate with them in matters of national defence of this hemisphere, and we are their best customers. I believe that the question of a corridor road through Maine, if properly presented, will not only receive their blessing but also their financial assistance, as it will be opening up and improving a section of their country for further development. The proposals I have mentioned required a dynamic, national attitude on the part of the present administration in order for them to be carried to fruition. When completed, they would shorten the truckers' route for products from my constituency to Montreal by some 250 miles. This would provide an alternative shipping route for our industries on a more competitive basis than presently exists.
It is a known fact that our long established Maritime industries have acquired and retrained national markets primarily through freight rate assistance. It is equally clear that some of our industries face extreme economic hardship unless the present scale of freight rate assistance is basically increased or steps are taken, as suggested, to shorten the competitive highway route to our central Canadian markets. Canada and this Government have no choice but to find ways and means to take the Atlantic Provinces into economic as well as political Confederation.

Bennett during the mid-1930's it was felt that because of the large geographical area of Canada, with a very small population, only a publicly operated broadcasting system could adequately serve the Canadian people. In some ways the C.B.C. has performed a wonderful service to the Canadian people, and it will undoubtedly continue to do so. In order to ensure that political interference will not take place, the C.B.C. has been so organized that it is not responsible to the Government, but rather to Parliament as a whole. The result has been that the C.B.C. would appear to think that they are responsible to nobody at all, and literally does what it pleases. I object to that attitude. to free expression of opinion. There seems to be a firm resistance by the C.B.C. officials to accept any kind of criticism or suggestion. Creativity in the Corporation is being stifled and it could turn into a fat, self-perpetuating, selfservicing bureaucratic Goliath.

speechtext:
The Address-Mr. M. Cote
In its October 8, 1964 edition, the newspaper Le Droit stated that about 2.5 million Canadians, that is over 13 per cent of the population, lived in extreme poverty and that another 1.5 million barely had enough to subsist.
In its April 1965 edition, Chatelaine magazine had an article entitled:
Poverty is the lot of over 4 million Canadians who lack the bare necessities of life. It read as follows: In 1965, a flourishing year if ever, over 4 million Canadians live in hardship, are ill-housed, ill-fed, ill-clothed and poorly educated. This state of affairs is to be found everywhere, in cities as in the country. However, the paradox is the same for all the underprivileged, regardless of where they live: the absurdity of suffering hardship in a land of plenty. Twenty-two per cent of the population barely has the strict minimum. In the province of Quebec, 25 per cent of rural families live in poverty and 45 per cent barely have enough to keep body and soul together.
So, now, the Government recognizes that our requests were quite reasonable and that those statistics, which put Canada in a bad light, were correct. And it seems willing to put an end to general poverty. In my opinion, that is the main point in the Speech from the Throne.
It was a pleasure for me to listen to the mover, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin), and the seconder, the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien), of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. While I am at it,
I should like to congratulate them most sincerely for having shown us the ill-effects of the lamentable state of the Canadian economy and the urgency of finding the remedies required.
All those testimonials were confirmed by the Prime Minister himself, who gave us an extremely lucid analysis of this chronic evil which brings shame upon our Christian democracies.
Of course, the plain truth is quite different from the wonderful statements made by the Minister of Finance in Toronto on February 1, 1965, as reported in Le Devoir:
As a matter of fact, stated the minister, 1964 was the best year in Canadian history. This is not the result of a mere chance. The policies of the Liberal government have directly contributed to those results.
I feel that the Minister of Finance, who is a chartered accountant, as everybody knows, has been deluded and misled by figures.
Naturally, the figures indicating the national product are steadily increasing, and this is quite normal because every year the population increases on the average by


345,000 citizens, through births and immigration. Yet, this does not mean that the economy is thriving. It will thrive only when those 4 millions of destitute Canadians will be able to enjoy a better distribution rather than redistribution of the wealth of Canada.
Family allowances, which could have been a most powerful instrument to balance family income, have remained at the same level since 1958 although they should have been raised in keeping with the rise in the cost of living. At present, there are 4,800,000 families in this country; what steps have been taken to support Canada's, greatest asset, our children? Nothing, absolutely nothing. Such is the result of the administrative carelessness of our governments under the control of financial oligarchy.
To adjust our national economy and eradicate poverty and misery, the government proposes certain measures which seem to have a socialistic approach. I am convinced that the government does not intend to lead us to socialism which destroys human qualities. However, with the projected implementation of all those plans, the one being more complicated than the next, I wonder what they are driving at, because that will not provide any equitable solution to the problems of family heads or of Canadians who do not have enough purchasing power to live decently. On the contrary, I do say that such plans will increase our general difficulties because they are detrimental to the freedom of initiative and enterprise and an act of aggression against individuals.
Why, Mr. Speaker, should we be made to fall out of the frying pan into the fire when it would be possible, with some minor adjustments to the finance mechanism of the country, to enable the Bank of Canada to issue new credits or bank money at administrative costs according to strict standards in order to meet the social needs of the people and make the public investments required for the development of the country?
It is the only way to hold in check our ever increasing debt. During the year the national debt will exceed $26 billion. The interest charges on that debt of the Canadian government will reach $1,102 million. Who will foot the bill for those interest charges? Small wage earners and middle income employees, to a large extent, will have to deduct this amount from their purchasing power, while they do not have an income related to the inflationary costs of living.
April 9. 1965
It is also disturbing to see such figures and to know that the government will have to deduct such an amount of money from the national budget to enrich private or commercial banks. Instead of that amount being paid in interest, it should be added to the budget of the Department of Public Works, which has to manage with the ridiculous amount of $208 million to meet the capital expenditures of our large country. It is really a distribution in driblets.
As an illustration, let us take the county of Chicoutimi which I have the honour of representing. This year we -would need to spend at least $20 million in public works, because the sea wharves are falling to pieces; we need a bridge to cross the Saguenay river at Chicoutimi; retaining walls and embankments should be built to protect the properties along the Saguenay river; sea relays, post offices, wharves at various places, etc., should also be built. We have enough men, materials and machines to do it, but we lack bank credits, bank money.
Is there anything stranger than being so helpless because our governments lie at the mercy of an out of date financial system which prevents us from taking advantage of the huge wealth accumulated by our ancestors?
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
By what means does the government intend to pay back that debt of $26 billion? When shall it be done? The speech from the throne says nothing about that calamity for the Canadian taxpayers.
Where are we going, Mr. Speaker, with that all-devouring usury which ruins our fellow citizens, undermines our economic foundations and is the underlying cause of that inflation which depreciates our money?
I wonder why the Liberals as well as the Conservatives are so afraid of talking about monetary reform, when Chancellor Ludwig Erhard, one of the most prominent statesmen in the world refers to it more than a hundred times in his essays on political economy, namely "Prosperity for everyone" and "A policy of affluence".
When Mr. Erhard came to Canada last June, the Prime Minister himself paid tribute to him, as reported in the July 1964 edition of External Affairs:
The part he played in the stupendous recovery of Germany is well-known and has gained our respect and our admiration.
It is difficult to imagine a higher praise. In addition to the elimination of poverty, the speech from the throne mentions amend-
The Address-Mr. M. Cdte ments to the Bank Act and the Bank of Canada Act.
I hope that this will mean that the issue of bank money or of credit will be nationalized and that the exclusive power of such an issue will be vested in the Bank of Canada alone. However, I think that the commercial banks and caisses populaires should keep the privilege of rediscounting bankable bills to the Bank of Canada at administrative cost, so as to meet industrial and commercial needs.
It is extremely important that this sovereign privilege of the state, that is the issuing of credit, be used for the common weal and not to the advantage of a few greedy people, actuated solely by their own benefit, ambitions and interests.
I also assume that the government does not wish the interest rates of the commercial banks to be increased, since those financial institutions are already reaping enough profits with a simple reserve of 8 per cent. The rate of interest on bank loans must be limited to 5 per cent, in order to stop this pernicious inflation which constantly sops the value of our currency. There should be limits to this devastating usury which, since the seventeenth century has spread throughout the whole world. A simple arithmetical calculation shows that if any new currency must return to the issuer with interest, there will come a day when all free economies will have been devoured by this usury and when the issuers of new credit-in this instance the commercial banks-will be the only holders and the absolute masters of money.
In days gone by, currency and credit were the sole prerogative of the king. The state reigned supreme. The mandate of the federal state is to provide for the welfare of every Canadian citizen. There cannot be two sovereigns at variance with one another: one reigning by natural right, stemming from the God-given power, and whose duty is to provide for the well-being of his subjects;-the other one reigning solely to exploit the Canadian citizens, to his own advantage, and actuated by the passion of his own interests.
Today, in Canada, there is only one real sovereign; it is neither the parliament nor the government, but the commercial banks, entitled every year to issue more than a billion dollars of new credit, whereas these regalities should be the exclusive right of the federal government, through the Bank of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, if, within the next ten years the Christian democracies do not recover con-



April 9, 1965
The Address-Mr. Beer trol over their monetary system, and it the latter remains based on interest and profit, we will be subdued by the communist powers. This is the serious warning I am giving to the hon. members of this house.
We, in this house, are mostly Christian parliamentarians and we ought to give the world an example of an administration based on justice and equity in which the economic mechanisms operate harmoniously for the well-being of every Canadian.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind the house that next September the Canadian section of the Interparliamentary Association will welcome in this Parliament building the delegates of 75 foreign countries who will be coming here to discuss problems of mutual interest. In our age of sociometry, it is easy to understand the interdependence of peoples and the significance of such a world conference.
A very elaborate program has been prepared to welcome those distinguished visitors. It will be a meeting of nations, prior to the marvellous gathering on the Land of Men, the 1987 World Fair in Montreal.
The Interparliamentary Union was formed in 1889 and it is the oldest and most important group of its kind. Since its inception, the two official languages of the Union have been French and English. This is worthy of note, for Canada may be the only country in the world to have both French and English as official languages. By that time, our federal services and indeed our civil servants should faithfully reflect the Canadian constitution. Special efforts and firm measures are essential to the correcting of those deficiencies which we observe practically every day at the various levels of our parliamentary system. I think my English speaking friends would also be fed up, and rightly so, if they came up daily against unilingual French speaking civil servants.
Therefore, we see what leading part our country will be able to play before those honoured guests who will come here to get ideas and means to improve the lot of their own fellow countrymen. That is why, Mr. Speaker, this parliament has such a heavy responsibility during the coming months and until 1967 for building an economic and social structure that will be on a par with men of ability and will arouse the admiration of the world.

The level from which we now view the needs of the Canadian people is very different from the sodden flats into which we dug our heels in 1963. The climb has not been an easy one because there have been those who would tend to obstruct and confuse the measures that were presented by the Government. My only claim on behalf of the Government is that a new confidence, a new purpose and a new determination, have been established in the minds of our people which have made our recent achievements possible.

If we had talked about transferring trade from the United States to the United Kingdom in

speechtext: Agriculture has undergone a very considerable technological change in the last ten years. We have moved into mechanized farming. This has had a very serious effect on agriculture as it is practised in Canada, because there have been areas which lent themselves to the use of mechanized equipment to a greater extent than some other areas of Canada. These areas were blessed with a tremendous production advantage. At the same time, there were areas in Canada which, because of their lack of adaptability to equipment and machinery, were placed at a tremendous production disadvantage. This brought about a great disparity in the income position of farmers in Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext:
There is no doubt that vertical integration may have played some part in this particular problem that exists. Farmers are not now content to have a declining share of the consumer's dollar. This is one of the problems that has confronted agriculture in recent years. Farmers wish to participate in the affluent society which many of us enjoy to a greater extent than they have in the past.
What are some of the benchmarks that prevailed when this Government took office? Earlier I mentioned the decline or reduction in essential services to farmers. We all, of course, remember the premium on the production of quality hogs which was placed on an on-again-off-again-gone-again-Flanagan basis. Then, I mentioned earlier that farmers were simply told to cut down on their production or the supports would be cut off. No attempt was made to curtail or look after the mounting surplus of butter, which by the

April 9, 1965
The Address-Mr. Beer time this Government took office amounted to 239 million pounds.
This Government believes that the problems confronting agriculture fall into three or four main categories. We believe, first of all, that the use of money has become increasingly important to many of our Canadian farmers. We think that the efficient use of land and machinery is extremely important and that management is one of the key figures in a successful farm operation. Management, which may be regarded as purely or partially educational, would immediately fall into the jurisdiction of the Provinces, because they do look after educational matters. However, the other matter of making money available to establish a viable economic unit is a Federal responsibility, and this has been undertaken. I need only mention two or three of the measures which have been enacted or placed on the statute books by this Government in order to make more money available to farmers.
We recall, of course, that during the last session amendments were introduced to the Farm Credit Corporation Act which doubled or practically doubled the amount of money that was available to farmers, up to $55,000 on a supervised loan. This made available the kind of money farmers needed in order to integrate their operation and make it an economic unit. I know that Members opposite and on this side of the House as well will be interested in knowing the extent to which this measure has been beneficial to farmers, and the extent to which it has been used. At the moment, we have 47,427 loans to farmers in Canada for a total amount of $434,556,153.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Possibly of particular interest is one comparison I would like to present, namely the increase in the number of loans this year as compared with last year, and I shall give this by provinces. In British Columbia last year there were 112 loans, and this year there are 200. In Alberta last year there were 614, and this year there are 982; in Saskatchewan 486 last year, and 799 this year; in Manitoba 125 last year, 220 this year; in Ontario 397 last year, 570 this year; in Quebec 324 last year, 379 this year, and in the Atlantic area 24 last year as compared with 48 this year, a total increase from 2,082 to 3,198. This is an increase of 53 per cent over last year in the use of the money made available.
It goes to indicate that the Government was right in arriving at the decision that making
(Mr. Beer.]
more money available to farmers would enable them to increase the size of their units and make them more economical.
Another comparison which may be of interest to hon. Members is the number of loans approved this year as compared with last year. In 1963-64 there were 8,689 loans approved, while this year 10,142 were approved, a 17 per cent increase; but the more interesting fact is that the size of loans increased by 43 per cent, thus showing that the amendment to the Act, by which more money was made available to farmers, was a step in the right direction.
In addition, the Government amended the Farm Improvement Loans Act, raising the ceiling on loans from $7,500 to $15,000. Farmers can now obtain this amount of loan from their banks, and it will be backed by the country.
I mentioned earlier that the use of machinery was one of the major costs to farmers, and the Government felt something should be done in this particular area. During the last session of Parliament a measure was introduced, known as the Farm Machinery Syndicates Credit Act, and I know the House will be interested in a brief report on the extent to which that act is meeting the needs of farmers. During the debate on supplementary estimates a number of questions were asked, and I think this report may answer some of these questions.
It indicates that the number of loans made available to syndicates has been one in B.C., 10 in Alberta, seven in Saskatchewan, one in Manitoba, two in Ontario and one in Quebec. In other words 81 members are participating in 22 syndicates and the total amount of loans involved is $215,404. I believe the House will warmly receive the news that this measure has met with general acceptance across the country and is filling a great need. One application has been received for the maximum amount of $100,000. This syndicate is in Alberta where a number of potato farmers have proposed joining together to buy washing and grading equipment for potatoes in the hope that they may do a better job of marketing the product on their farms.
As has often been indicated by the Minister, another thing which affects farmers materially is the danger of crop loss, and in order to meet this contingency the Government brought in a measure to amend the Crop Insurance Act, whereby the Government of Canada can underwrite Provincial schemes
April 9, 1965
that may be introduced. All these measures have helped meet the needs of the farming community by way of providing capital and protecting farmers against some of their losses.
As the House well knows, improvements which affect farmers are introduced by legislation, some of which I have indicated, by Order in Council, or by administrative means. Members on all sides of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak in the debate on the Speech from the Throne. The last time I spoke in a similar debate was back in 1958, and I must admit

192	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Skoreyko that this was indeed a long time ago. At the outset of my remarks I want to congratulate the hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) and the hon. Member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien) on the manner in which they discharged their responsibilities to this House as Mover and Seconder of the Speech from the Throne. As young Members,
I congratulate them, and I am sure their constituents will be proud of the responsibility they have shown.
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks I wish to say that rather than being critical for the sake of being critical, I want to offer some constructive criticism to which I hope the Government will pay some attention and will heed. I cannot help, of course, but refer for a moment to the speech made by the hon. Member for Peel (Mr. Beer). It has been a long time since I have listened to a dissertation so politically biased as the one completed just a moment ago. I dare say that even his constituents know that the hon. Member for Peel is not capable of writing such a document, and I might ask him where he got his information from.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I did not mean to transgress any rule; I was just making an observation. The reason I made it, of course, was that when the hon. Member for Wellington South (Mr. Hales) rose and asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture, who should be able to come up with the answers immediately, "Does the hon. Member believe that it was a good idea to remove the quota on turkeys?", he said, "There will be another opportunity to answer these questions". This is what we have heard since this Government took office: There will be an opportunity at a later date.
I became involved in a debate last Friday over the very same thing. The hon. Member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) stood on his feet and said that we should not be talking about the estimates of the Department of Labour, when we were in fact dealing with

DEBATES	April 9, 1965
that very Department at the time, and the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) said there would be ample opportunity subsequently to answer these questions. Then I asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture whether he thought that the legislation which removed the capital grants from fairs was good legislation, and whether he thought the 11 per cent sales tax was good legislation. I believe that if he wanted to be honest with the House he would rise in his place and say, "No, it was not good legislation; but I was not responsible for it".
This afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with the many items in the Speech from the Throne, and I hope to review later the proposed legislation item by item, if time permits. But I want to offer something constructive to the Government. I suppose that because I have a number of items with which I wish to deal this afternoon, the first thing I should start with is the question of amnesty in so far as the Chinese in Canada are concerned. I have before me a clipping from the Montreal Gazette which states, in part, that when the former Minister of Citizenship and Immigration the hon. Member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Tremblay) was asked whether the amnesty covered all the cases in which the Chinese might be involved, he said that illegal passport cases were not covered, and being smuggled into the country was not covered.
I agree that in a good many cases people who were smuggled into Canada or entered this country illegally should not be covered by the amnesty; but I think it is entirely wrong to search out Chinese who have lived in Canada for eight or ten years after entering this country on an illegal passport. In many cases these people who entered Canada were not even aware of the seriousness of this infraction of the law. However, these people have lived in this country for eight or ten years, we are now searching them out and they are still under the impression that they will be prosecuted. I suggest to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Nicholson) that the proper action for him to take would be to search out those culprits who issued or were responsible for the issuance of the fake passports in the first instance. The Minister should immediately issue a press release clarifying the Government's position in respect of this matter and let those people- there are undoubtedly hundreds of them- still remaining in Canada, who are afraid of
April 9. 1965

the consequences, come forward and make a declaration so that they may become honest, law-abiding citizens of Canada.
I have here a clipping from the Calgary Albertan of September, 1964, which is very interesting. This was written shortly after the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration advised the House that the deadline, in so far as he was concerned, for amnesty would be September 1. I say it is a fortunate thing for those Chinese who have since sworn declarations as to their true identity that the House of Commons was in session at that time, otherwise the amnesty may have been cancelled.
Mr. Speaker, I say that there are inadequacies within this amnesty program of ours. For instance, as I pointed out a moment ago, the people who came into the country on illegal passports are not covered by it. The article in the Calgary Albertan says:
L. C. Hawkins, regional immigration director, says about 1,100 illegal immigrants have come forward to claim amnesty since the program was started.
He estimates another 2,000 remain in hiding. Some 500 are the forged-passport cases.
Ingrown fear of police action, prosecution and deportation keeps some from coming forward, he believes.
"This, coupled with the fact that the amnestry does not cover the illegal passport cases, is a real problem", he said.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I have heard the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration in recent days-as a matter of fact, today-make it clear to the House, or at least I understood it to be a clear statement, that the Chinese people in the country who have not as yet made a declaration have nothing to fear, excepting those persons who could be charged with smuggling or offences in connection with narcotics. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that in most cases the Chinese who are in this country today by reason of having entered on illegal passports do not realize the seriousness of the offence. The Minister should make a statement forthwith to the press which would enable these people to come forward and clear their names. In a statement which appeared in the Edmonton Journal of August 14, released under an Ottawa dateline, the former Minister of Immigration is reported to have said:
Henceforth from September 1, 1964, the R.C.M.P. and immigration officers are being instructed to apply the law to Chinese in exactly the same way as to other residents of Canada.
He also said-and this puzzles me somewhat-that he was having some difficulty about recent cases where people had been smuggled into Canada. I say there should be no problem at all in this respect. As I
The Address-Mr. Skoreyko understand it, the amnesty covered those Chinese who entered this country prior to the amnesty program. Anyone who entered this country after that time was fully aware of the law and of the consequences of breaking the law. As I say, I hope the Minister will consider a press release defining clearly, once and for all, the limitations and the extent of the amnesty program.
I notice with interest that the Speech from the Throne contains another promise that the Immigration Act and the Citizenship Act will be revised. I wonder when these revisions will take place. I want to quote from page 24 of the report or memorandum submitted to the Government on March 10, 1965 by the Canadian Labour Congress. Maybe I do not agree with everything the Canadian Labour Congress enunciates but I certainly do in this case. They say:
We have consistently criticized the Immigration Act and the administrative procedures under it. We have done so for many years and find a growing number in Canada who share our concern over the legislation and the way in which it is administered. As we have said before, we consider the Immigration Act clearly discriminatory in tone in so far as the selection of immigrants is concerned. Past practice has made this all too clear. The greatest preference has been given to immigrants from the countries of Northwestern Europe. Different criteria seem to be employed with regard to prospective immigrants from other parts of Europe and elsewhere. Although the regulations have been amended in a way which would seem to mitigate the effect of the provisions of the Act, we are not altogether satisfied that this is so. It is still possible for immigration officers to select immigrants not on the basis of the contribution they can make to the life of the country, but on the basis of their pigmentation or some such reason.
I agree wholeheartedly with the recommendations which are contained further on in this memorandum. Though I will not take the time of the house by putting them all on record I advise the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to peruse this particular document carefully.
It may be suggested that the Canadian Labour Congress has not made a thorough study of the Immigration Act and does not therefore fully understand the subject with which it is dealing. For my part I have made an extensive study of the act and of the regulations since I arrived here in 1958. The former Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, Mrs. Ellen Fairclough, who is unfortunately no longer a Member of this House, did somewhat broaden the regulations affecting admission to Canada. Notwithstanding these efforts, discrimination has not been com-
April 9, 1965

The Address-Mr. Skoreyko pletely eliminated from the regulations. Somehow, in some way, it persists. Although the old section 20 of the Act, with its paragraphs (a), (b), (c) and (d), are supposedly no longer in existence, it is still being applied by immigration officials. I thought the new regulations of January 19, 1962 constituted a wonderful improvement. Part I dealt with admissions and part II with the jurisdiction of the appeal board. The hon. Lady said at that time:
The most important provision of the new regulations is section 31 which is in fact the core of Canada's immigration policy. The new regulation 31, replacing section 20 of the former regulations, lays primary stress on education, training and skills as the main condition of admissibility, regardless of the country of origin of the applicant.
I have just said, and I say it again, that although section 20 is no longer in existence it is still being applied.
One of the things I do not understand about the Immigration Act is why I can sponsor relatives, no matter what their qualifications may be, from countries such as Great Britain and the United States while I cannot sponsor them from countries in Asia and certain parts of Europe. I realize there are difficulties surrounding migration facilities in Europe. On the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration I asked the Minister whether he would consider staffing our embassies, in countries which do not allow us immigration facilities, with competent people from the Department of Immigration who could assist our embassy staffs in processing applications approval of which would unify families in Canada. I have not yet had any response to this suggestion but I hope the Minister has it under consideration and that it will be mentioned in the white paper which the hon. Gentleman said he will be introducing before long.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The requirements under section 31 are simply these, as I understand them: first, an immigrant has either a profession or a trade; second, he has either sufficient financial capital to establish himself in Canada or he has relatives in Canada willing to guarantee his maintenance. In so far as I am concerned those are the two things which can be taken to be the criteria of acceptance and admission into Canada. Although these criteria apply to many other countries, they do not apply to several countries, and I take exception to the continued use of this old section 20. I should like to know why the Immigration Department has the right to

deny individuals of Asiatic origin or with skins of different colour the right to apply for and obtain permission to bring relatives to Canada under the existing regulations.
I hope the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Nicholson) will change his attitude and do some of the things we have asked him to do in order that this situation can be changed. I suggest that he should look at these regulations in a broad sense and realize the many hardships which are being imposed on people of many ethnic origins in Canada. These people originally were quite happy with the immigration laws as they exist, but many have found after visiting immigration offices in different towns and cities that certain of their relatives cannot qualify for entry into Canada.
I should like to ask one question for the purposes of clarification, Mr. Speaker; but before doing so, in order to give a clear picture of the situation to which I refer, I should like to quote from page 12324 of Hansard where the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Badanai) quoted from a statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) at a press conference on December 31 of last year. This quotation reads as follows:
I have asked the minister to prepare a white paper on immigration policy, immigration administration and immigration procedures, telling what has been done and what is in process, and to have that available if at all possible-and it is possible, I think-by the beginning of the next session of Parliament.
This is that next session of Parliament referred to by the Prime Minister, and even if the white paper was tabled this afternoon, so far as I am concerned, it would not only be days overdue, but years overdue. I do not criticize only this administration in this regard, but all administrations for not having taken action to eliminate the discriminatory sections of the Immigration Act. I should like to know now when this white paper which was promised is to be brought forward.
I have dealt with these promised changes because of the many statements which have been made in the Press regarding this unfortunate state of affairs. I should like to quote the headline of an article which appeared in the Montreal Gazette on September 24, 1963, which is: "Favreau Promises Change in Chinese Immigration". I need not remind the House of the fact that there has not been any change made in respect of Chinese immigration.
I should like to quote also from an article which appeared in the June 25, 1964, edition
April 9, 1965

of the Toronto Globe and Mail under the heading "Chinese Offer Tremblay Food for Thought". According to this article Mr. Tremblay said there would be a general overhaul of immigration policy. The article states:
He hinted also at a coming general overhaul of immigration policy and announced that he will go on a tour of Canadian immigration offices in other countries, including Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Portugal and Greece.
"I shall go on the journey at the recess of Parliament-if we have a recess," he told a reporter.
We did not have a recess so I assume he did not make that trip.
The article then states:
Improvements in immigration procedures that were made as a result cut down the waiting period for sponsored relatives from nine months to three, Mr. Tremblay said.
I remember that not many years ago there was a list of some 250,000 people in Italy who wished admission to Canada. That was indeed a long list. Those individuals have conducted themselves in a manner that is acceptable to the Canadian way of life and we should do something that will assist in expediting the processing of these applications.
The Minister also dealt with changes in the Hong Kong immigration office. He suggested that they were going to expand the facilities there in order to take care of the backlog of applications from that area of China for entry to Canada. On January 18, 1965, only a short time ago, a headline appeared in the Montreal Gazette which read, "Canada Establishes Long Term Policy for Immigration". I suggest that all hon. Members should read the article under that headline. I read it and experienced some anticipation in respect of new policy on the part of the Department of Immigration. The article in part stated:
The reorganization of the department also includes steps to:
Make immigration posts abroad more effective.
Improve the pay of immigration officers abroad.
Give officers at home and abroad more responsibility to make decisions on their own initiative, a step to speed the handling of immigration applications.
Improve the morale of Immigration Department employees by giving them the prestige accorded career diplomats.
I might say that this whole article dealt with the reorganization of the Immigration Department policy, and these are the changes which were announced. I suggest it is not enough to make changes of this kind while at the same time leaving the impression with the public that new immigration policy is being established. These four recommended changes relate only to internal matters and

Someone suggested that this was straight propaganda, and I must say that I agree.
In concluding my remarks in respect of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration let me say that I hope the promised white paper will be produced soon and will contain revisions similar to those recommended.
At this time I want to make one or two comments regarding the work of the Bilingualism and Biculturalism Commission which has done nothing more than conduct uncertain studies across this great country of ours. I use the term "uncertain" because up to this time that Commission has confined its studies to how English and French speaking Canadians fit into the Canadian way of life.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
No one seems to be particularly concerned about the other one third of the population of this country comprising the other ethnic groups. I am not going to dwell on the B and B Commission at any length, but I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that any massive concession by any government to any minority group in Canada would just be the beginning of many problems. I say this only because there are some one million Germans in this country, some 750,000 people of my national origin, some 450,000 to 500,000 Italians, and so on down the line. I do not think that you can build a united Canada by recognizing one or two races as the only races in this country. They must all be recognized as they have been in the past. I simply say that it will be very interesting to see the final report of this Commission, because I think it has done nothing more than to sow the seed of uncertainty in this country, which we could have very well done without.

Mr. Speaker, since I have not sufficient time at my disposal to sum up Mater et Magistra, I would suggest that the hon. member read the chapter which deals with socialization.
It is comforting to find that no aspect of the social and economic life of this country has been neglected and that nobody seems to have been forgotten in the speech from the throne submitted to our examination.
The government's desire to keep on following the course it set itself is clearly reflected in this legislative program, which shows us to what extent the government is conscious of the needs and fondest aspirations of the Canadian people and how it can take into account, in its legislation, the problems facing us now.
Thus, we find the government quite intent on waging war on poverty, through programs and policies designed to provide every Canadian, no matter which area and province he comes from, with a decent income. I refer to grants to workers forced to move to new jobs, to the training of workers for industry, etc.
As regards administrative reforms, there are proposals to overhaul the Bankruptcy Act, the Bank Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act and the Citizenship and Immigration Act.

That, Mr. Speaker, is the third phase of the program worked out only two years ago yesterday by the party to which I have the honour to belong and which was ratified by the Canadian people. Already, after only two years of administration-

If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote an editorial from the newspaper he Droit of April 3, 1965. It is entitled "End of a session", under the signature of Marcel Gingras:
In spite of filibustering which marked its proceedings, the session now coming to an end was much more fruitful than would seem at first glance. There is no intention to give a list here of the 95 pieces of legislation passed since February 18, 1964, but we cannot ignore some facts as important as the adoption of the flag, the adoption of a national pension plan, the enactment of the labour code, the agreement on the opting out formula concerning shared cost programs or the integration of the armed forces.
Mr. Speaker, representing as I do a district which has greatly suffered in the past from its remoteness from the great centres on which our governments focused all their attention-I might add that it also suffered from the indifference of our various administrations and the inertia of some of our representatives-I can only welcome the fine program outlined in the speech from the throne to improve the standard of living of underprivileged Canadians. The Gaspe area, I do not hesitate to say it here, really became economically active only when a dynamic and progressive government took office in Quebec in 1960. That government restored its true meaning to the autonomy behind which its predecessor had hidden for 16 long years, thus depriving the people of the province and those of the Gaspe area in particular, of major sources of capital which were indispensable to the economic recovery of those underprivileged and depressed areas and

The numerous efforts of this federal government since 1963 to restore the economy of areas like mine, by enticing industries to settle there, have given a shot in the arm to the Canadian economy and some hope to the people. To mention only one, that of designated areas, I can say that this policy has been a determining factor of the establishment in New Richmond, in my riding, by the Bathurst Power and Paper Company, at a cost of almost $50 million, of a wood processing factory which will be in operation in August 1965. The construction itself, since last April, has been giving work to about 900 people. When it is in operation, this industry will provide steady and well paid jobs to almost 1,000 Gaspe people and to several Canadian experts, not to mention the many opportunities which the increase in the population of this town will bring to businessmen, farmers, workmen and professionals in my area.
At the same time the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), in co-operation with the said company, is also making, at a cost of almost $1 million, very important improvements in port facilities which will assist the shipping of the products of this new factory to the domestic and exportation markets. Without the strong measures initiated by this government, jointly with the equally strong efforts of the Quebec government and of the Bathurst Power and Paper Company, the latter would not have made such a decision and our area would still be waiting impatiently to take its place under the sun.
It is encouraging to see that the speech from the throne mentions the intention of the government to extend to other areas of the country this policy of special conditions to designated areas. To do that, he should alter the criteria on which this measure was based, criteria which I criticized in a constructive way at that time.
I believe that the data obtained from the unemployment insurance offices, though quite valuable for the government in the assessment of underdeveloped areas, do not do justice to those areas in our country where there is practically no industry. Though far from large centres, the Gaspe peninsula, for instance, and the county of Bonaventure especially, offer many facilities and opportunities which should attract industries: their proximity to the sea, inexpensive means of transportation and available manpower which 22620-14
will be soon skilled and ready to work. These factors, combined with an urgent need for industry and a high rate of unemployment, should be taken into consideration by the experts during the review of designated areas.

Incentives will have to be found if we want not only to preserve but to develop the tourist industry, one of the main sources of income in the Gasp6 area. I am thinking, for instance, of the establishment of a regular air route to Gaspe. Besides tourists, the planes could transport the mail so that news would not be outdated when it reaches us. As I pointed out very often here to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), that would require the improvement of existing private landing strips by the government. In view of the time at my disposal, I must omit a number of important points, but I should like, however, to stress the importance of developing the seaport of Gascon. This parish has the greatest number of fishermen in the county and little or no other sources of income. Therefore, I hope that the special conditions granted to designated areas will apply in this case and enable those fine people to establish a fish processing plant so as to process locally and to their profit the fish they wrest at the cost of hard work from the sea.
Our municipalities and seaside residents suffer also from the policy of the Department of Public Works with regard to erosion damage caused to private properties by the sea. Private individuals and municipalities are financially unable to build those costly retaining walls which have become necessary. Such an emergency should prompt the government to revise its present vexatious policy.
Those are the few remarks I wanted to make in this debate, Mr. Speaker.
