Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity of speaking on the Throne Speech and I would be remiss if, at the start, I did not congratulate the Mover and the Seconder of the Address in Reply on the fine job they did last Tuesday.
The Throne Speech did not make mention of any proposed attempt to increase our export trade and we in this Party are very concerned about our imbalance of trade with the United States. I believe we should examine the reasons why we are not securing more of the United States market, and in this connection I would like to put the figures for the last eight years on record.
In 1956, under the then Liberal government, our imbalance of trade with the United States was $1,167 million. This was reduced in 1957, the first year the Conservative government came into power, to $996 million. By 1958 we had reduced this another $400 million, to $564 million, or by $550 million since the last year of Liberal government. In 1959 it was further cut to $527 million and in 1962, the last year the Conservatives were in power, it was $544 million.
The projected figure for 1964 is close to $728 million, representing an increase of over $200 million during the short time since the Liberals returned to power, and present policies indicate they are driving for a figure of over $1 billion to be soon achieved in our trade imbalance with the United States.
Canada is losing ground in trade. The Canadian economic report has stated Canada's share of world trade is declining. The bulk of our exports is still resource material, although the big boom in world trade has been in manufactured goods. The lion's share of Canada's exports is still going to the United States and Britain, but everywhere Canada is losing ground to other countries and other exporters. These disquieting facts emerge from the Economic Council of Canada. Mr. Speaker, the Economic Council
[Mr. Bechard.1
stated that the aim for better economic products is to win better access to foreign markets for Canadian manufactured products and highly-processed raw materials, instead of concentrating, as in the past, on tariff breaks for raw materials. Elsewhere in the report the Council noted that manufacturing will have to supply most of those 1,500,000 jobs needed in Canada between 1964 and 1970. They also pointed out that future Canadian prices and costs must be kept in line with any given exchange rate and with world prices and costs for goods entering into the international trade. What has the Liberal Government done about this?
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The Council also said the private institutional psychological barriers to higher exports of manufactured goods must be reduced. Steps recommended in this direction are broader development within Canadian industry of modern and aggressive marketing techniques; adequate, competitive, export financing facilities; removal of arbitrary restraints, where they exist, on the competitive export capabilities of foreign-controlled firms; vigorous trade promotion for industrial goods. It is a known fact that world markets for manufactured goods are increasing, and we must share in these markets if we are to maintain existing standards of living and to provide employment that will be needed in future years. Every effort should be directed to the expansion of secondary manufacturing.
I	have asked questions regarding the 11 per cent sales tax of the Finance Minister (Mr. Gordon), the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) and in every case the Ministers' replies are very vague, sometimes pointing out that exports are increasing or that economy is good; but they are afraid to face up to the issues. They will not admit that this tax is hurting our Canadian exports. These figures that I have given today show that the imbalance of trade with the U.S. is going to be over $700 million this year. While the Conservative Party when it was in power cut this drastically, this Liberal Government is letting it slip right back to where it was- over $1 billion in 1956. The point is that these increased costs on building materials, on processing machines, on industrial machinery, must be borne by the Canadian citizen. The loss of export business, the loss of Canadian jobs, the high cost of Canadian goods and higher operational costs mean high finished goods selling prices. High finished goods
April 9, 1965

prices mean limited sales, and limited sales naturally impose limits on production not only for food processors but for all those industries serving this country.
This environment limits the Canadian labour force and the amount of money this force can pay to the Government in the form of income tax. Certainly the high cost of production curtails drastically the number of foreign markets. As a matter of fact, the primary reason a great percentage of our total exports have been on the increase is that we receive preferential treatment from our best customer, the Commonwealth. Collectively the United Kingdom and Commonwealth countries account for our exports being as healthy as they are. Canada has been warned about the imbalance of trade which they have with the United Kingdom. Harold Wilson has warned countries that they are going to be very firm regarding imports.
In the January issue of the Canadian Food magazine they had this to say: "Is the Canadian politician against us? Canadian and U.S. tariff comparisons are not fair. The 11 per cent sales tax legislates against competitive, domestic and export pricing". They also stated that a probe should be conducted on assistance by foreign Governments on export pricing. They pointed out that Canadian industry should be watching very carefully the negotiations that will be going on at GATT this year. This is where general agreements on trade policies will be set up for the future. The late President Kennedy recommended a cross-the-border cut on all present tariff structures.
I feel our Canadian export delegation at GATT should be very careful with these tariff reductions until this Government sees fit to reduce taxes that are hurting our export trade. We must also consider the standard of living in this country as compared to other countries that we will be asked to trade with; and we must in addition consider our climate conditions in Canada, which is a factor in our costs of production.
However, as if these natural factors were not enough to retard the efficiency of Canada's food processors in both domestic and foreign markets, the present Government has further compounded the problem through the additional burden of an 11 per cent tax on new building and machinery. What this artificial burden does to our building and equipping costs is quite staggering. Some examples cited in their brief are as follows: A food processing machine in the U.S. costs about
The Address-Mr. Stenson $12,000; the same machine in Canada costs over $16,000. A labelling machine costing $59,000 in the U.S. costs the Canadian user $75,000. A case packer going for $11,730 in the U.S., in Canada calls for an investment of $15,000; and a case unloader going in the U.S. for $8,000 goes for $11,295 in Canada.
On everything the Canadian processor touches, from agricultural products through to packaging, from new machinery to building bricks, he is faced with much heavier costs than his U.S. counterpart. Yet he is expected to sell efficiently against his U.S. opposite in foreign markets, and also defend his domestic position-all in spite of the present obvious tariff imbalance.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to read from an article that appeared in the Peterborough Examiner regarding the Fisher Gauge Company. You have heard of this in the House before; it is the company that has gone to the United States because of the 11 per cent sales tax. This article says:
New York state governor Nelson Rockefeller is scheduled to tour the Watertown operations April 1.
The Fisher brothers, Chester and company president William, still seem somewhat awed by the rapid growth and potential of their operation.
"We are now working on developmental projects with several major U.S. manufacturers," Chester said, "and if our ideas are accepted it may mean substantial growth in the near future.
The potentialities are staggering."
But both men are disgusted and discouraged by the Dominion governments' attitude toward Canadian manufacturers.
William Fisher said the Dominion government gives special consideration to the raw materials industries (mining, pulp and paper) but is persecuting the manufacturers whose employment is much greater.
The climate for manufacturers is good in Europe, even better in the U.S. and Fisher expects business soon from Australia.
But Canadian government policies, Mr. Fisher stated, are driving manufacturers from this country.
"While our growth is most encouraging," William Fisher said, "it is certainly not nearly as rapid as woul dbe possible if the climate for industrial growth was more favorable."
The 11 per cent tax on production machinery led to the founding of the Fisher plant in Watertown last year and the tax is still a big headache for the company.
The complexity, the red tape, the import duties and the duplication of taxes between both senior governments has necessitated increased office staff and hours of work for senior company officials.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
In New York State, Mr. Fisher explained there is no sales tax on industrial equipment.
Here, he said, there is tax on purchase and tax on harbour, both governed by a complex set of rules.
Chester Fisher said the growth of the Watertown operation was unexpected, partly because
April 9. 1965

The Address-Mr. Stenson
Americans would rather buy products made in their own country than those imported.
Sometimes we wonder whether this Government would like to see everything imported for our use.
We have heard from several hon. Members with regard to the car parts industry. I, too, feel I should bring to the attention of the government the fact that all across Canada people are becoming alarmed about the trade agreement which has been set up. I refer particularly to the car industry agreement. What effect will these agreements have on our car parts industry? The Minister has told the manufacturers that they must cut their costs. It is a known fact that this agreement was reached down on President Johnson's ranch. I think this is a very queer place to be signing an agreement which will affect many of our workers in Canada, especially those engaged directly in the car parts industry.
Canadian-owned industry will suffer. This is one industry we should be trying to promote and help at the present time. Other manufacturers affected are those who are trying to operate in this country with United States capital. Canadian industries have been told to cut their costs or they will be deprived of this business. This is what the minister told us in this House. How can these industries cut their costs when every time this Government turns around it raises taxes?
I would like to ask the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) why he has tied the Canadian Government to this free trade policy when the United States government has not given approval to the plan. I know the Minister is aware of the statements which have been made on this subject and the attacks which many of the auto parts makers have levelled at this Government with respect to its trade policy. A firm in Ingersoll has made a statement through its president that the plan signed on January 16 by the Prime Minister and President Johnson means his company will have to pull out of the auto parts manufacturing business if the agreement is not revised. A questionnaire mailed to members of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers Association of Canada indicated that most of them are unhappy about the provisions of this scheme. Evidence has been placed before the minister that manufacturers of auto parts are being denied the privilege of bidding on business transacted with the Chrysler plant in Windsor.


The Minister has stated in this House that manufacturers of car parts must become more efficient. However, as one auto parts manufacturer pointed out to him, if one is not given a chance to participate in this large United States market, how is one to become more efficient? Every car parts manufacturer in Canada is worried about this trade agreement the government has made. The manufacturers feel the Canadian Government must give serious attention to the situation in which this industry finds itself, and reconsider this trade agreement.
Under the automobile plan set up by this government, $50 million of Canadian taxes or money which would normally have gone to the Department of National Revenue will be given to the large car manufacturers as a subsidy. The Minister of Industry has not seen fit to make any attempt to help our car parts manufacturers, with the result that many will be forced out of business. That will be the result of this agreement, the result of this policy adopted by the Liberal Government. Instead of decentralizing large industries, hon. Gentlemen opposite seem to have a policy of centralizing them.
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes at my disposal I have outlined the fears of industry and labour in connection with our export markets and I would urge this Government to seriously consider the removal of these detrimental roadblocks.

speechtext:
should like to pay my compliments to the hon. Member for Westmorland (Mrs. Rideout) on her lovely speech the other day. We have a community of interest, since we were elected at the same time and I was very pleased to hear her excellent speech. She graciously acknowledged that the image of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) played a leading role in her election. For my part I should like to point out that the image in Canada of the hon. Member for Bumaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) played a leading role in mine.
We in the New Democratic Party take some satisfaction in the Speech from the Throne, in the sense that after so many years of prodding from this side of the house the Liberal party has finally taken the first hesitant steps toward a program of manpower utilization.
The manpower policies set out in the Speech from the Throne are not, as has been said, a challenge to the bold; rather, they are little more than a sop to the timid.
April 9, 1965	COMMONS
The Government could have opened a new chapter in Canadian history, it could have provided the solid confidence needed to usher in the scientific age of automation and cybernetics. Instead it has given us warmed-over old hat. The Government could have given this country confidence for the future by the use of a simple clearcut statement in the Speech from the Throne such as: This Government commits itself to the proposition that policies will be designated to guarantee full employment in Canada. There can be no real gain in the economy of the nation until a Government dedicates itself to this basic fundamental proposition.
The greatest concern of Canadians today is the fear of unemployment and the related problem of economic growth. Until this fear is allayed, economic development will lag. Until Government makes a commitment to full employment, the economy will fluctuate from uncertainty to uncertainty. The Government had this opportunity. They either did not recognize it, or they muffed it. Canadians had been waiting for a clarion call, but got instead sour notes.
There probably was a time when government could say that such an objective as full employment was impossible. They do not dare say that today, because we know better. We know, and there are people at the disposal of the nation who know, that these objectives are obtainable, if only the proper course of action is taken. It needs only a determination on the part of Government to make full employment a policy. The people of Canada would do the rest.
This commitment would not have cost the Government a cent; yet such a commitment to the people of Canada would have been of the greatest psychological effect. Confidence in the future would spur spending on both consumer and capital goods. We hoped for this clarion call but got the Speech from the Throne instead.
Much has been said and written about the progress made in Canada's manpower programs during the last few years, especially since the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act came into effect in 1961. At first observation, one is likely to be impressed by the number of new training schools built, the students accommodated, the placements of workers, etc. But we have been impressed, not because it has been done well, but because anything has been done at all.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
There seem to be two schools of thought about the nature and causes of Canadian un-
DEBATES	203
The Address-Mr. Saltsman employment. Most economists tend to blame inadequate demand, particularly inadequate consumer demand. When purchasing power and willingness to buy is not keeping pace with our country's capacity to produce goods and services, cut-backs develop in production, workers are laid off. These further reduce demand. They are followed by more cut-backs and lay-offs, not only in the consumer goods industries but also in those producing heavy machinery and equipment. So came high unemployment and sluggish economic growth. The gap between our ability to produce goods and services and the ability of people to buy those goods and services is reflected in unemployment. The solutions proposed are designed to raise and maintain aggregate demand. They may range all the way from modest proposals regarding the interest rate, to a whole constellation of programs including large scale Government expenditure on social capital, lower taxes for middle and low income groups, and greatly expanded social security programs. These are solutions that we propose, but not the solutions that are seen in the Speech from the Throne.
The second school of thought senses that unemployment takes the form, not of an absolute gap between the supply of and demand for labour, but rather, a mismatching between the labour demanded and the labour supplied. They feel that there are enough jobs to go around but not enough Canadian workers possessing the necessary skills, or in the right places, to fill all these jobs. Thus, job vacancies on a large scale may co-exist with unemployment on a large scale. This mismatching or imbalance in the labour market is produced by structural changes in our economy, due mainly to rapid technological change and to new trade and tariff policies. Technological change, it is said, creates new jobs while destroying old ones, but the new jobs require a higher level of education and technical know-how. Both technological change and new tariff policies may cause the location of job opportunities to change by producing a rise in new industries and a decline in old ones, or by encouraging greater concentration of production facilities.
The New Democratic Party feels that the fundamental cause of Canadian unemployment has been due mainly to inadequate demand. In the past we have proposed a wide range of policies designed to build up purchasing power and to keep it growing in balance with
April 9, 1965

The Address-Mr. Saltsman
productive capacity. We shall continue to advocate these measures in the future because, in spite of the improvement in economic conditions since 1961-62, there are still no long-run forces in our economy which can guarantee a continuing state of buoyant demand. Wheat sales to Iron Curtain countries, and devaluation of the dollar cannot be relied upon indefinitely. Deliberate Government policies of an expansionary nature-particularly large scale Government expenditures on social capital and reduced taxes on low income groups-are essential.
However, it also seems to us that over the next decade or two the mismatching kind of unemployment will grow in importance as technological change accelerates. To cope with the problem we will require an active, co-ordinated, manpower policy; it will lie with the monetary and fiscal authorities and will be a collective responsibility of Government. The objective of manpower policy will be to achieve balance in the labour market and maximum utilization of manpower resources under given conditions of demand.
There are many weaknesses in Canada's present manpower policy. Three of them have overriding importance. First, it lacks coordination. Second, there is no continuation of analysis of changes in the composition of demand for labour. Third, there is no satisfactory program to aid and encourage the geographic mobility of workers.
Mr. Speaker, no manpower policy can hope to succeed without co-ordination of the various programs of which it consists. Canada's manpower policy is scattered among a variety of agencies and branches, even among a variety of Government departments. The Economic Council of Canada has called attention to the fact, charging that "lack of coordination of manpower services is a basic weakness of labour market policy in Canada", and warns that, "to distribute such tasks to separate branches and agencies will only succeed in rendering impossible an integrated labour market program".
First, all manpower programs ought to be in one department-logically the Department of Labour. Those departments such as Citizenship and Immigration that now operate placement and other manpower services ought to transfer these to the Department of Labour. But even within the Department of Labour, co-ordination has been lacking. There are now at least five agencies in the Department engaged in manpower policies.
[Mr. Saltsman.1
Mr. Speaker, we do not suggest that these agencies should lose their identity but that their functions should be clearly defined and co-ordinated. With regard to the Manpower Consultative Service, the Economic Council has said:
It is hard to escape the impression that it is a disembodied branch, and not at all integrated into an over-all labour market program.
Mr. Speaker, to achieve the necessary coordination and direction in manpower policy, one of the manpower agencies should build their activities around it. The logical agency for this role is the National Employment Service, because of its continuous contact through its 200 or more local offices with local labour markets. The Economic Council of Canada has made exactly this point. They have said:
The N.E.S. must become the key operational agency for implementing manpower policies. It must also become the sole co-ordinating agency of all programs and policies related to the labour market.
In announcing the transfer of N.E.S. to the Department of Labour on March 31, the Minister made some encouraging remarks in this regard, stating that steps would be taken to ensure that the Employment Service would become the key operational agency in the manpower field.
The Minister has wandered hither and yon on manpower policy since he took office. One hopes that he is now on the right path, to stay. On January 26 in St. John's he said that he was delighted with the part of the Economic Council's report dealing with manpower policy. Then on March 8 in this House he unleashed an attack on the same section of the same report. Now he is back giving cautious endorsation to part of the manpower policy advocated by the Council. We can only hope that his confidence in the Council's recommendations will grow, and that the foundations for a solid manpower policy in Canada will be developed. I hope that the Liberal Government makes a better job of this than some of the agencies have done, where very often their efforts have seemed to be much like a Wagnerian death wish. If this Government wants a good manpower policy for Canada and wants the N.E.S. to be successful, it should be prepared to go out and hire the proper people at good salaries to make sure that this will occur in Canada.
The most incredible thing about Canada's so-called manpower policy is that it is
April 9. 1965

operated in a vacuum of labour market information. There is no agency of Government that carries out a continuous and detailed analysis of changes in the composition of demand for labour. The N.E.S. is structurally equipped for this job on the basis of its local offices. But it has been starved for funds and professional staff. It has been unable to carry out this function. For example, there is provision for only one economist in the N.E.S. and even this position has gone vacant for five of the last eight years because the salary offered is too low to attract a professional person.
When Ministers talk glibly about changing
the supply structure of the labour force in accordance with changes in labour demand, one gets the impression they know what types of labour are going to be needed. But they do not know. Nor is there any agency of Government which is carrying out the kind of continuous analysis and forecasting that would enable us to know.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
How can we possibly discuss the courses to set out for our vocational schools if we have no notion of the kind of labour market that these students are likely to face? How can we devise training courses to upgrade the adult labour force or to train the unemployed if we do not have a clear picture of the kind of labour services currently demanded by industry, or likely to be demanded over the next several years? Technical training that takes place in a vacuum of labour market information is an exercise in futility. The same is true of programs designed to assist the moving of workers. It is a classic case of the blind leading the blind.
Training and mobility programs, to be effective, must be integrated into an active, national, labour market policy. An essential foundation for such a policy is a continuing analysis and forecasting of labour market demand.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, we feel that this could be carried out through the National Employment Service, possibly in conjunction with the Economics and Research Branch of the Department of Labour. Through its local offices throughout the country the N.E.S. could get advance information from most of the country's employers of expected changes in the level and composition of their demand for labour. This information should then be analysed by a professional staff. When certain trends are discovered the information should then be fed to the training schools so that
The Address-Mr. Saltsman they would be able to arrange their curricula in accordance with labour market trends. There should also be assessment as to the utility of questions. In other words, let us not ask pointless questions, as has so frequently been done in the past. Let businessmen who are going to be asked these questions know why the questions are needed, and let them understand the value and merit. There would be a lot less opposition to the answering of questions.
Structural change in our economy will require a high degree of geographic mobility of the labour force to adjust to the changing location of job opportunities. In a country of Canada's size financial considerations may pose a serious obstacle to a worker who considers a move. A comprehensive program to provide financial assistance for worker mobility is therefore urgently required. There is only a smidgen of such assistance in Canada at the present time. The programs that we have had in the past have fallen dismally short of what has been done for many years in most of the countries of Western and Northern Europe.
The New Democratic Party proposes that a national labour mobility program be launched based on the following principles:
(a)	That it include not only assistance for the travelling expenses of the worker, but also a removal allowance to help him in the moving of his family and belongings and a settling in allowance to help him get established in the new region. It should also include a second residence allowance for workers attending a training school away from home.
(b)	Assistance should not be based on a means test.
(c)	It should be truly comprehensive in scope. In other words, its provisions should not be confined to disadvantaged workers in depressed areas but should be available to all workers in any part of the economy, including workers moving on a temporary basis.
(d)	The assistance should be administered and co-ordinated by the National Employment Service which, through its local offices across the country and its constant contact with local labour markets, is the only agency in a position to carry out this function.
The New Democratic Party manpower policy embraces the following: A co-ordinated set of manpower services built around the National Employment Service and performing the functions of a labour market
April 9. 1965

The Address-Mr. Saltsman board. This co-ordinated group of services might be called the national manpower services. It also includes a nation-wide network of adult training centres under the direction of the national manpower services. Allowances would be paid to unemployed trainees on a wage related basis. The federal government would pay 100 per cent of the cost of allowances and would set the levels.
Our policies are designed to move Canada into the scientific age while still preserving and heightening the human values upon which our society is founded. For the first time in human history the prospect of plenty for all is possible, plenty not only for Canadians but for all humanity. Automation and cybernation can be that avenue, that road, that highway to plenty for all people. But to take advantage of the fruits of science the Government must commit itself to a manpower policy designed to ensure full employment. Otherwise fear will put roadblocks in the way of progress. Only if full employment is assured will the workingman lose his fear of change. It is easy enough to tell the workingman he has nothing to fear, but when he knows he has a wife and children to look after or if he is contemplating marriage or is concerned about his future, fear is a very important factor. If the Government is really concerned about those factors that go toward making for slowdowns and featherbedding in industry, then it will move to remove the fear of unemployment from the mind of the workingman. The workingman functions best when he is not afraid of the future, and a Government proposal to maintain full employment would remove that fear from his mind.
Only a worth-while manpower and investment program can ensure that the change into the scientific age will take place with ease among those in industry and will not meet with resistance from industry. People who have worked all their lives to build and maintain a business are justifiably afraid of the kind of changes that are taking place in society. I think they are quite willing to change and quite willing to meet the new challenges, but the opportunity to rationalize their business operations should be available to them through an increased amount of capital machinery so they can compete with others in the same market. If the Government accepts this challenge, this land can be free from fear and ready for the scientific age.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY JUSTICE MINISTER RESPECTING CORRECTIONAL REFORM

speechtext:
The Minister of Justice, the Honourable Guy Favreau, today announced to the House of Commons details of two measures foreseen in last Monday's Speech from the Throne. Both measures concern correctional reform and are part of the Government's plans to modernize Canada's entire treatment of offenders. Speaking in the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, the Minister outlined the Government's intentions on:
(1) The Special Committee on Corrections: a group of specialists to be named shortly in addition to the joint Parliamentary committee on corrections already proposed on the Order Paper.
(a) Terms of Reference: as now approved by Cabinet, the Terms of Reference of the Special Committee on Corrections are as follows: "To study the broad field of corrections, in its widest sense, from the initial investigation of an offence through to the final discharge of a prisoner from imprisonment or parole, including such steps and measures as arrest, summonsing, bail, representation in Court, conviction, probation, sentencing, training, medical and psychiatric attention, release, parole, pardon, post release supervision and guidance and rehabilitation; to recommend
as conclusions are reached, what changes, if any, should be made in the law and practice relating to these matters ih order better to assure the protection of the individual and, where possible, his rehabilitation, having in mind always adequate protection for the community; and to consider and recommend upon any matters necessarily ancillary to the foregoing and such related matters as may later be referred to the Committee; but excluding consideration of specific offences except where such consideration bears directly upon any of the above mentioned matters." (2) The Free Vote on Capital Punishment: In order that Members of both Houses of Parliament may have at their disposal all the elements necessary to make a truly free and informed decision on the possible abolition of capital punishment, the Government will publish an Information Paper on this subject. The Paper will present objectively, without taking any determined position, all significant facts and arguments advanced by both defenders and opponents of abolition. It will contain notably a brief history of capital punishment, statistics showing its apparent value or irrelevance as a deterrent, and notes on the experience of other countries.
Monday, April 12, 1965
